description: CAD bake-off 3 of 3 -- BLENDER: build the SO-101 gripper assembly parametrically in cad/blender/. SHARED CONTEXT (same task, three tools, one pebble each so they can run in separate git worktrees): recreate the SO-101 gripper assembly -- the fixed jaw (gripper body) and the moving jaw -- as a baseline for comparing three CAD tools. Jake verbatim: "I want to be able to modify them in the future, so you will have to do it in a way that supports that." That means parametric, editable source. Importing a mesh and calling it done FAILS the test. Use named variables for every dimension that might plausibly change: jaw length, jaw opening, fingertip thickness, servo horn bore, fastener sizes, wall thickness. DIMENSIONAL SOURCE OF TRUTH -- two real SO-101 STEP files are already committed at cad/build123d/reference/: Moving_Jaw_SO101.step and Wrist_Roll_Follower_SO101.step. STEP carries exact analytic geometry, so measure from these. Do NOT re-download them and do NOT invent or eyeball dimensions from tessellated meshes. WHY THIS PART: it is what Jake will modify for the Hand 1.0 paper gripper -- cross-reference plans/hand_1_0.md and plans/gripper_bet.md as reading, and cite them in your notes. DELIVERABLE BESIDES THE MODEL: a NOTES.md in your own tool directory covering time taken, what was easy, what was painful, whether the tool known weakness actually mattered in practice, and how it would feel to modify this part six months from now. State plainly if the geometry ends up approximate and list what still needs verifying. BOUNDARIES: stay inside your own cad/<tool>/ directory and touch nothing else. Do NOT edit plans/hand_1_0.md or plans/gripper_bet.md -- a later pass writes the comparison across all three tools. The other two tool pebbles are running in parallel in their own worktrees, so do not touch cad/openscad/, cad/build123d/, or cad/blender/ other than your own. TOOL SPECIFICS: Blender is at /Applications/Blender.app and runs headless via /Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender --background --python <script>. THE CRUX FOR THIS ONE: Blender is NOT parametric CAD, so the only way to meet Jake requirement that the part stay modifiable is to build it from a bpy script with a named-parameter block at the top -- re-running the script regenerates the model. Hand-modelling a mesh and saving the .blend does not count. Deliver the bpy script, a PNG render, an STL export, and the saved .blend, all produced headlessly. Read dimensions from the reference STEP files at cad/build123d/reference/ (measure only -- write nothing into that directory; if Blender cannot read STEP directly, say so in NOTES.md and describe how you got the numbers without inventing them). VERDICT SHOULD BE EVEN-HANDED: note fairly where Blender genuinely wins -- rendering, visualization, and the fact that the existing Tool Caddy scene already lives in Blender (plans/tool-caddy.blend) -- alongside where the lack of parametric CAD and B-rep hurts. MID-FLIGHT CLARIFICATION (added 2026-09-13, AFTER this pebble was claimed and work had started -- read it even if you are already mid-run; it changes what you optimize for, not what you build): WHY WE ARE DOING THIS (the goal is not the gripper -- the goal is choosing the tool). Recreating a part that already exists produces nothing new on its own. Its entire value is as a controlled benchmark. Jake is about to design Hand 1.0 (a paper-handling gripper that mounts to the SO-101 and is also usable handheld) and later Hand 2.0 (a fully 3D-printed human hand identical to its teleop glove). That is a long hardware design programme and it should be done in ONE tool. This exercise decides which one. WHY RECREATE A KNOWN PART SPECIFICALLY: because there is ground truth. The reference STEP files say exactly what the geometry should be, so "did this tool let me express the real part accurately" has a checkable answer -- unlike designing something new, where any result looks plausible and you learn nothing about the tool. WHAT IS ACTUALLY BEING MEASURED (optimize for producing a fair verdict, NOT for finishing fast): (1) Can this tool express real mechanical geometry accurately, from measured dimensions? (2) How painful is it to change a dimension six months later? This matters MORE than initial build speed, because these parts will be iterated many times against measurements that do not exist yet. (3) Does it live well in git -- readable diffs, reviewable history? (4) Can an AGENT author and revise it directly? Jake wants to iterate hardware by voice, which means the format has to be text an agent can reliably write. (5) Is the output actually usable for functional printed parts -- fits, fillets, fasteners, bearing seats? (6) It must be open source. That was Jake's stated requirement. THEREFORE: an honest NOTES.md verdict is the PRIMARY deliverable, equal in value to working geometry. An agent that hits a genuine wall and documents it precisely has done this task correctly. Do NOT paper over friction to make your tool look good -- a tool that loses fairly here saves months of pain later. This decision feeds plans/hand_1_0.md (section 6 records the provisional OpenSCAD-first call that this exercise is meant to confirm or overturn) and plans/gripper_bet.md -- read both, cite them, and still do not edit them. FOR BLENDER SPECIFICALLY: judge it against all six criteria even where it is obviously weak -- it is not parametric CAD and has no B-rep, which hits (1), (2) and (5) hard. Be equally fair where it genuinely wins: rendering, visualization, and the fact that the existing Tool Caddy scene already lives in Blender (plans/tool-caddy.blend). A clear loss documented precisely is a correct outcome for this pebble.
test_instructions: cad/blender/ contains a bpy script with a named-parameter block at the top covering jaw length, jaw opening, fingertip thickness, servo horn bore, fastener sizes and wall thickness, and re-running it regenerates the model
A PNG render, an STL export and a saved .blend are committed, all produced via Blender --background --python

cad/blender/NOTES.md covers time, easy, painful, whether Blender not being parametric CAD actually mattered here, where Blender genuinely wins (rendering, visualization, existing Tool Caddy scene), six-month modifiability, and what still needs verifying
Dimensions trace back to the reference STEP files rather than being invented, and cad/build123d/reference/ is unmodified
Nothing outside cad/blender/ is modified -- in particular plans/hand_1_0.md and plans/gripper_bet.md are untouched

results.identified_issue:
APPROACH. Blender has no STEP importer and no OCCT binding. Rather than invent dimensions, I installed cadquery-ocp into cad/blender/.venv (gitignored by the repo's existing cad/*/.venv rule) and used it strictly as a measuring instrument: no geometry was authored with it, and cad/build123d/reference/ was only ever opened for reading (verified with git status). I also wrote measure_step.py, a dependency-free ISO-10303-21 parser, so a future agent can re-read the references without the venv. Both readers agree.

WHAT I VERIFIED. fixed_jaw 65.20 x 52.00 x 105.35 vs reference 65.200 x 52.000 x 105.425; moving_jaw 22.36 x 92.00 x 48.00 vs 22.300 x 92.000 x 48.000. Hole diameters (3.2 / 2.0 / 1.5 / 5.4 / 6.0 / 5.4 / 10.0 / 20.0 / 24.0), the 4x M3 on a 14.0 mm PCD at +/-4.95 shared by both parts, the 45-degree chamfers, the 0.75 edge break, the 20.0-degree fin lean and the 6.03-degree moving-jaw face tilt are all read out of CYLINDRICAL_SURFACE / PLANE / CONICAL_SURFACE / TOROIDAL_SURFACE entities.

THE BIG UNRESOLVED THING, and the most likely place I am wrong. The two STEP files are isolated part files in unrelated poses; there is no assembly transform to recover. Worse, each part carries TWO candidate gripping faces: (a) a large flat face -- 642 mm^2 on the fin, normal (0.94,0,-0.342), offset -48.162; 656 mm^2 on the moving jaw, normal (-0.994,0.105,0), offset -10.0 -- with a line of five 1.5 mm holes exactly 5.0 mm in from it; and (b) on the opposite side, a staircase of +/-45-degree planes at exactly 10.0 mm pitch along the finger, the SAME pitch as those holes.

I chose (a). Evidence for (a): a large flat contact patch plus a 5 mm inset hole line is what pad retention looks like. Evidence for (b): serrations facing the workpiece is the classic gripper jaw, and the pitch match means each hole sits at a step. A future agent should know that (b) is live, because it changes which SIDE of the fin the moving jaw swings on.

CONSEQUENCE OF CHOOSING (a). The flat face sits 10.06 mm from the moving jaw's pivot and about 26 mm from the fixed jaw's at the same height. Those cannot both hold for a jaw that closes flush, so at jaw_open_deg=0 the fingers overlap near the root (visible in out/so101_gripper_closed.png). I tried the alternatives before settling: flat-close on the -X side puts the pivot at x=-51.8, outside the part; flat-close on the +X side puts it at x=-22.4, inside the fin. Neither works, which is itself evidence that one of my two face readings is wrong. I also tried a boolean interference sweep over pivot_x and pivot_z (fit2.py approach): interference never approached zero on the -X side, 6800-13600 mm^3 across the whole range, because the moving jaw's 33.4 mm fork gap cannot straddle the 48 mm-wide cradle.

WHAT I FITTED RATHER THAN MEASURED. pivot_z=24.35 and wrist_centre_y=-0.218 ARE measured (midplane of the servo's own M2 holes at z=14.100/34.600, and the wrist-roll horn centre). pivot_x=-25.54 is chosen so the fingertips meet: 82.01 mm from the fixed tip at (-12.9, 105.375). mj_closed_lean_deg=8.84, fin_pivot_to_face=15.82 and fin_tip_s=80.44 all fall out of that choice. They are frozen constants, NOT expressions -- change mj_finger_length and they are silently wrong. First job for whoever picks this up is to turn them into expressions.

DELIBERATE OMISSIONS. The 26 + 34 B-spline faces (organic hub-to-finger blends) are replaced by straight tapers between measured stations, so the silhouette is right and the surface is faceted. The 10 mm staircases are measured but not modelled. The servo cradle is a plain U with the measured wall positions and M2 pattern, no internal ribs. The gripper servo itself is not modelled, so nothing checks that it fits or that the fork clears it. fin_width_table was sampled by ray-casting the tessellated reference in 5 mm Z bands -- good to a few tenths, no better.

BPY GOTCHA worth recording: object.matrix_world is stale until the depsgraph updates, so composing a transform from a freshly-set .location/.rotation_euler silently discards the placement. That produced a plausible-looking wrong assembly early on. Build the matrix explicitly.
results.summary: Built the SO-101 gripper in Blender as a bpy script with a parameter block, so re-running it regenerates the model, render, STL and .blend.
results.detailed_description:
cad/blender/so101_gripper.py is the source. A ~60-entry parameter block at the top holds jaw length, jaw opening, fingertip thickness, servo horn bore, M3/M2 sizes and wall thickness; the code below lofts and booleans both jaws from those numbers. ./cad/blender/build.sh rebuilds out/ headlessly, and you can sweep a value without editing the file: --set jaw_open_deg=0 --set mj_finger_length=110.

Blender can't open STEP, so I measured the references outside it two ways -- a dependency-free parser of the STEP text, and OCCT in a throwaway venv used purely as a ruler. MEASUREMENTS.md maps every parameter to the entity it came from. Both parts now match the reference bounding boxes to about 0.1 mm. cad/build123d/reference/ is untouched.

One thing I could not settle from the two files alone: which face of each finger is the gripping face. Each part has a big flat face with insert holes 5 mm in from it, and a 10 mm-pitch staircase on the opposite side. I went with the flat faces. The cost shows in the closed render -- the fingertips meet but the fingers overlap near the root, which means either my pivot is a few mm off or the staircases are the grip faces.

Read NOTES.md for the full verdict. Short version: about 2.5 hours, and well over half of it was reverse-engineering the assembly rather than modelling. Blender genuinely wins at rendering and at understanding a part you did not author -- I recovered the assembly pose by rendering guesses and looking -- but there are no fillets, no constraints, no STEP out, and the derived constants are frozen numbers that will rot.

The measurement that would settle it is already on your list: where the gripper servo's output axis sits relative to the fixed jaw's face, on the real arm.
